notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2034.tlg003.1st1K-gr: 2.38: τῶν ἐρχομένων (‘those who come’) makes no sense here and is taken as τῶν ἀρχομένων, ‘those they govern’. The text’s οὖ (2.38 twice, 2.40) and οὐ in 2.40 (‘and again the masses’) are read as αὖ, ‘again’. 2.39: τῶν φαινομένων (‘the visible [ones]’) is taken as the visible gods, the heavenly bodies; πλέον τῷ παθητικῷ νέμοντες (‘occupying … more through their passible part’) is obscure. 2.40: the words in square brackets are bracketed in the edition, probably as a gloss. 2.41: καθʼ ἕνα μὲν γὰρ οὐκ ἔσθʼ ὅτε οὐχὶ … οὐκ ἀνιᾶσι has too many negatives and is probably corrupt; taken as ‘never slacken’. 2.42: κακοδαίμονες (‘the wretches’) literally means ‘those with evil daimones’, probably a deliberate pun.
οὐ δύναται μέντοι διὰ παντός has no expressed subject; taken as the precaution not availing at all times, though it may mean that sorcerers cannot keep it up throughout.

nodes.text: But since the notion of them is confused and has come into great discredit, it is necessary to distinguish their nature by reasoning. For perhaps, they say, it is necessary to show where the error about them arose among human beings. The distinction, then, must be made in this way. All souls that have sprung from the universal [soul] and administer large parts of the regions beneath the Moon, resting upon a *pneuma* [the breath-like body of a soul] but controlling it by reason — these must be considered good *daimones* [spirits ranked between gods and humans], and be held to do everything for the benefit of those they govern, whether they preside over certain animals, or over the crops assigned [to them], or over the things that exist for the sake of these, such as rains, moderate winds, fair weather, and the other things that work together with these, and the good tempering of the seasons of the year; or again, for us, over the arts and the things of music, and all education, and medicine and gymnastics and anything like these. For it is impossible for these both to provide benefits and in turn to become causes of harm in the same matters. Among these must be counted also those who, as Plato says, ferry and carry messages from humans to gods and from gods to humans, bearing up our prayers to the gods as to judges, and bringing out to us their exhortations and admonitions together with oracles. But all souls that do not control the *pneuma* joined to them, but are for the most part even controlled by it, are for that very reason driven and carried about to excess whenever the angers and desires of the *pneuma* take their impulse. These souls too are *daimones*, but they may fittingly be called evil-working.

And all of them, both these and those of the opposite power, are invisible and wholly imperceptible to human senses. For they are not clothed in a solid body, nor do they all have one shape; rather, the forms that give their *pneuma* its character, being impressed in many shapes, at one time appear and at another are invisible; and sometimes the worse ones even change their forms. The *pneuma*, being bodily, is subject to affection and perishable; and though it is bound by the souls in such a way that their form endures for a longer time, it is nevertheless not eternal. For it is likely that something continually flows off from it and that it changes. The [*pneuma*] of the good ones, then, is in due proportion, as are also the bodies of the visible [gods], while those of the evil-doing ones are out of proportion; and these, occupying the region about the earth more through their passible part, leave no evil that they do not attempt to do. For having a character that is altogether violent and treacherous, and deprived of the protection that comes from the higher daimonic [power], they mostly make their assaults vehement and sudden, like ambushes, sometimes trying to escape notice, sometimes using force. Hence the sufferings that come from them are acute, while the healings and correctives that come from the higher *daimones* seem slower. For everything good, being tractable and even, proceeds in order and does not overstep what is due. If you hold this opinion, you will never be able to fall into the greatest absurdity, that of supposing evil of the good and good of the evil. For not only in this respect is the account absurd, but the many also, taking up the meanest notions about the gods, spread them to the rest of mankind as well.

For this too must be counted as one [part] of the greatest harm that comes from the evil-working *daimones*: that although they themselves are the causes of the calamities about the earth, such as plagues, crop failures, earthquakes, droughts and the like, they persuade us that the causes of these are those who are also [the causes] of the very opposite [that is, of good harvests], removing themselves from blame and making this very thing their first concern: to do wrong unnoticed. And after this they turn us to supplications and sacrifices to the beneficent gods, as though these were angry. They do these things and the like because they wish to move us away from the right notion of the gods and turn us toward themselves. For they themselves delight in all things that happen in this inconsistent and incongruous way, and, as if putting on the masks of the other gods, they profit from our folly, winning the masses over to themselves by inflaming human desires with loves and longings for wealth and power and pleasures, and again with vainglory, from which arise factions and wars and things akin to these. And most terrible of all, they go further from here and persuade [people] of similar things about the greatest gods as well, to the point of bringing even the best god under these charges, by whom, they say, all things have been turned upside down. This has happened not only to laymen but also to not a few of those who spend their time in philosophy. The cause has been mutual. For those of the philosophers who did not stand apart from the common drift came to the same [views] as the masses; and again the masses, hearing from those reputed wise things in harmony with their own opinions, were strengthened in thinking such things about the gods still more.

For poetry, too, inflamed people's notions further, by using a diction made to astonish and bewitch, and able to induce enchantment and belief about the most impossible things; whereas one ought to be firmly convinced that the good never harms and the evil never benefits. For it is not [the work] of heat, as Plato says, to cool, but of its opposite; so neither is it [the work] of the just to harm. And surely the divine is by nature the most just of all things, since otherwise it would not be divine. Therefore this power and portion must be cut off from the beneficent *daimones*. For the [power] that is by nature disposed and willing to harm is the opposite of the beneficent; and opposites can never come about in the same thing. While these [evil ones] ravage mortal nature in many parts, and sometimes in great ones too — for there is never a time when they are not doing so to someone — the good do not slacken in what is theirs to do, but also forewarn, as far as they can, of the dangers hanging over [us] from the evil-working ones, revealing them both through dreams and through a soul inspired by a god and through many other means. And if someone were able to distinguish what is signified, everyone would know and take precautions. For they give signs to all, but not everyone understands what is signified, just as not everyone can read what is written, but only one who has learned his letters. It is through the opposite [*daimones*], however, that all sorcery is accomplished. For those who accomplish evil deeds through sorcery honour these above all, and the one who presides over them.

For these are full of every kind of illusion and capable of deceiving through the working of marvels. Through them the wretches prepare love philtres and love charms. For all licentiousness and hope of wealth and of fame come through these, and above all deceit. For falsehood is proper to them; for they wish to be gods, and the power that presides over them wishes to be thought the greatest god. These are the ones who delight ‘in libation and the savour of burnt fat’, by which their pneumatic and bodily [part] is fattened. For this lives on vapours and exhalations, in varied ways through varied [offerings], and is strengthened by the savours of blood and flesh.

Therefore a man of understanding and self-control will beware of using such sacrifices, by which he will draw such beings to himself; and he will strive to purify his soul in every way, for they do not attack a pure soul, because it is unlike them. And if it is necessary for cities to propitiate even these, that is nothing to us. For by them wealth and external and bodily things are considered goods, and their opposites evils, while very little in them is concerned with the soul. But we, as far as we can, shall not need what these provide, but both with the soul and in external things we make every effort to become like god and those around him (which comes about through freedom from passion, a clearly articulated understanding of the things that truly are, and a life directed toward these very things), and to become unlike wicked men and *daimones*, and in general everything that delights in what is mortal and material; so that we too shall sacrifice in accordance with what was said by Theophrastus. With this the theologians too agreed, knowing that in so far as we neglect to remove the passions from the soul, to that extent we are joined to the evil power, and it will be necessary to propitiate it as well. For, as the theologians say, those who are bound by external things and do not yet master their passions must avert this power too; otherwise they will have no end of toils.

Therefore such precaution has seemed necessary even to sorcerers, though it does not avail at all times; for they trouble evil *daimones* [spirits ranked between gods and humans] for the sake of licentiousness. So purity was not a thing for sorcerers but for divine men, wise in the things of god, and it brings to those who practise it a safeguard everywhere: their affinity with the divine. Would that sorcerers too practised it always! Then they would not have been eager to practise sorcery, being shut off by it from enjoying the things for whose sake they commit impiety. Hence, being full of passions and abstaining only for a short while from impure foods, filled as they are with impurity, they pay the penalty for their lawlessness against the universe, partly at the hands of those very [beings] they provoke, partly also at the hands of Justice, who watches over all mortal deeds and thoughts. Purity, then, both inward and outward, belongs to a divine man, one who strives to fast from the passions of the soul and to fast also from foods that stir the passions, who feeds on divine wisdom and is made like [god] through right thoughts about the divine, who is consecrated by intellectual sacrifice and approaches god in a white robe, truly pure, of freedom from passion in the soul and lightness of body, not weighed down by alien and foreign humours and passions of the soul.
